It takes a village to run a Guild. It’s not just an old
saying, it’s the truth!
If you have some old tools or supplies you don’t
need, don’ be alarmed. We’ll have a spring clean in
May. The details to follow, but it is basically a half
day flea market and mini auction at Sapperton Hall.
The last one was a lot of fun as members got to liquidate their superfluous items and others got to fill
up their shop with stuff they never knew they needed!
The President’s Challenge for March is “before and
after”. Do you have a piece that sits around the
house, maybe for years, that you are not quite happy with? Maybe you are still trying to figure out
how to complete it – does it need colour, texture,
carving, bending or other abuse? To enter this
challenge is to submit TWO pics of the same turning. One of the half-baked piece; the other, the
completed masterpiece.
Steve

Fibonacci and the Golden Rule Of Thirds
Fibonacci rules, derived from the Fibonacci sequence, can be applied in various creative fields,
including woodturning. The Fibonacci sequence is a
series of numbers where each number is the sum
of the two preceding ones (e.g., 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8,
13, 21, and so forth). Here are some ways Fibonacci rules can be utilized in woodturning:
Proportions: The Fibonacci sequence can be used
to determine pleasing proportions for woodturning
projects. For example, the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approaches the golden ratio
(approximately 1.618), which is considered aesthetically pleasing. By using these ratios, turners
can create visually harmonious designs for bowls,
vases, or other turned objects.
Segmented Turning: Segmented turning involves
gluing together multiple pieces of wood to create
intricate patterns. Fibonacci numbers can be used
to determine the number of segments in a turning
project. For instance, a turner might use Fibonacci
numbers to determine the number of segments in
each ring of a segmented bowl or vase.
Design Elements: Fibonacci spirals and curves can
be incorporated into the design of turned objects.
For example, a woodturner might use Fibonacci
spirals to guide the shape of a bowl or the curves
of a spindle. These spirals can add visual interest
and elegance to the finished piece.
Spacing and Layout: Fibonacci numbers can be
used to determine the spacing and layout of features on a turned object. For instance, a turner
might use Fibonacci numbers to determine the
spacing of decorative elements such as beads or
coves on a spindle or the placement of feet on a
bowl.
By using Fibonacci rules in woodturning, we can
create pieces that are not only visually appealing
but also well-proportioned and harmonious. These
principles can help elevate the craftsmanship of
turned objects and provide turners with a framework for creating beautiful and balanced designs.
In woodturning, the rule of thirds (Fibonacci) can
be applied in several ways to enhance the aesthetics of turned objects:
When considering the overall composition of a
turned object, such as a bowl or vase, the rule of
thirds can help ensure that the object feels balanced and harmonious. By placing key elements
along the grid lines or at the power points, turners
can create a sense of unity and cohesion in their
work.
By incorporating the rule of thirds into our
woodturning practice, we can create turned objects that are not only functional but also visually
compelling. Whether designing bowls, vases, or
other turned forms, the rule of thirds can serve as
a valuable tool for achieving balanced and aesthetically pleasing compositions.

As woodturners, we occasionally (or constantly, if
you are a segmenter) need to be able to space features equally around the circumference of a circle.
Or possibly calculate the width of staves in a vessel,
even if we aren’t an out and out segmenter. As luck
would have it, that is often a number evenly divisible into 360 (degrees) but as we all know, luck isn’t
always on your side and you have to figure something out for 73 positions or pieces. Of course,
there are plenty of lathes with suitable index
wheels attached as well as aftermarket index
wheels that have a zillion segments, but they won’t
give you the correct width of a stave, for instance.
Recently I watched a video on calculating any number of segments in a circle between 3 and 100. One
and two are not included for obvious reasons; one
is a full circle and two is simply a line drawn
through the center. What caught my eye was the
“any number between 3 and 100” part.
Rather than simply present the link to the video I
chose to write a short article on it, mainly because
the presenter clearly didn’t understand that the
values in the table included in the article were not
measurements in inches but rather, simply trigonometric values. This created quite a bit of confusion.
Also, the constant reference to “inches” seemed to
rule out its use in the metric system (he, in fact,
ruled it out) or, for that matter, the “Marvin” system on Mars. A circle is a circle and the Greeks
pretty much sussed out the whole system around
them a long time ago (“around them” – see what I
did there? ). In general, he made the whole thing
a lot more complicated than it needed to be.
It took him 25 minutes to say, “Multiply the diameter by the constant for the number of segments
required to obtain the chord of each segment”.
That, in itself, is a bit of a mouthful but, understanding what a “chord” is will help. The chord of a
circle is a line perpendicular to the radius defined
by two points on the circumference. Wow, still a
bit much. OK, it’s the straight line of the piece of
pie that joins the curved portion of the segment. As
always, a picture is worth a thousand words.
If you know the length of the chord in a segment
you can step it off around the circumference of a
circle with the compass set to the length of the
chord. Simply set the compass to that measurement, start with a mark on the circumference then
“walk” the compass around the circle by advancing
the point of the compass to the next mark all the
way around the circle. Connect all those points to
the center and you will see that they are equal segments. (The fact that you ended up back where
you started from is a good indicator as well). It’s
hard to set most compasses to three decimal
points, so in practical terms you will typically incur
a cumulative error as you progress around the circle but by progressively adjusting the compass you
can nail it right on after a few trips around the
world. My guess is that the greater the number of
chords, the more you have to twiddle with the
compass. Typically, we are only interested in the
actual points on the circumference so if that’s the
case, at this point you probably have all the information you need.
(Continued on page 7)
The line A-B in the illustration is the

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
Example: Using the table below, let’s pick a number of segments other than something that divides
evenly into 360 (degrees): 7 segments. Let’s also
say the circle is 10 inches (or centimeters or
marvins) in diameter. If you multiply the diameter
of the circle by the constant for 7 segments you
will get the length of the chord in whatever unit of
measurement that you are using.
10 X .4339 = 4.339 (inches, centimeters or marvins)
If you had a cylinder and needed to mark 7 points
equidistant (4.339 inches) around the circumference it’s an easy task to step your compass around
the piece. Ta-Da! Understandably, there may be
some confusion between the flat sheet of paper
and the curved surface of the piece as far as the
compass (or dividers) are concerned, but with further twiddling to account for the point of the compass or dividers wanting to “slide into home”, you’ll
have what you need. OK, now to-da.
If you needed to know the major width of the
staves for your staved piece, the length of the
chord would be your measurement (typically your
outside diameter) then you have to bevel the sides
and that’s a whole other calculation, but not a difficult one if you’re prepared to take this project on
in the first place). Warning: the diameter of the
circle you should use would be obtained by extending the segment lines to intersect the tangent 90°
to the center point of the arc between the points
defining the chord. You can forget all that (I’m going to) and just make the width of the staves wider
than the chord by about 5%. In other words, you’re
in the ballpark, so fudge it.
I hope I didn’t hurt your head too much (that was
the whole point of this). Just another tool to keep
in the drawer for that one occasion where you
might choose to have 73 flutes on your porch columns.
(Continued from page 6)

This is a culmination of every steady rest I could
find in the net. The design is a comprise of realization of my welding skill, or lack thereof, and the
capability of size and strength. The outer ring is 1
1/2” square mild steel tubing and the roller assemblies are 1 1/4” . The maximum diameter that I can
it use is about 16” which although much reduced
from my lathe’s 24” swing is big enough for the
neck/tail stock end of most hollow forms.
The bar is 5’ of cold rolled 1 1/2” mild steel. The
length is long enough to provide good weight and
leverage but short enough to fit into my available
space at the end of the lathe. The 1 1/2” “D” extension has been replaced with a 1 1/2” steel tube
welded along side of the boring bar. This small lateral offset is enough to counter any twist as deep
hollowing is usually done without any offset of the
cutter head.
The cutters are mounted onto 3/4” exchangeable
inserts. The guarded hook cutter is Woodcut ProForme which is excellent at low stress stock removal. The scraper in the back ground is made from a
1/4” planer blade sharpened to 65 Degrees. I also
use a 3/16” square scraper for some jobs. The tool
rest is made up from old angle stock and has a
reach into a vessel of about 10”. The pin on top
provides a reference and stop to prevent the bar
coming off the rest. The LEDs at the end lead back
to a transformer and allow me to see what’s happening inside.
This set up is bastardization of one of Phil Vetra’s
creation. My modifications include a 24” maple
roller to handle the weight of the big bar and an
adjustable top bar to handle smaller diameter
bars. You will notice that the capture bar is supported on a swing away mount. As I’m not worried
about alignment, I think when it’s held tight up
against the lathe tube, the dowel alignment pins
are strong enough to hold the weight. I’m still
working on the laser set up (the top bar is too
heavy).
If you’ve got questions; fire away.

I made several versions of this form, considering
ways to stay balanced while moving, for example
while walking, stooping, or dancing. I started with a
rounded base that can wobble, and added a counterbalance on the top. A bent stem places the center of balance off to one side. It reminds me of
stretching out to reach a heavy object on a high
shelf.
This was my first attempt at combined turning and
bending. It’s interesting warping a turning so that it
is no longer symmetrical. It’s also a fun way to keep
working with a form after removing it from the
lathe.
I am excited that this sculpture will be included in
the AAW POP 2024 Showcase and Auction, travelling to Portland for the Symposium in May.
“Reaching Out”
Birch, 5.75 x 4.5 x 2.75”
My Bending Technique: Soak in very hot water for
30 minutes, then bend around a form and hold
with rubber bands until dry.

Where you will find more information about Paul
Russell:
https://paulrusselldesigns.com/
https://www.etsy.com/shop/PaulRussellDesigns
https://www.facebook.com/russellwoodz/
https://www.instagram.com/paulrusselldesigns_/
As summarized on his website, Paul Russell
“A transplant from San Diego to Utah, I’m a
maker of 35 years with a passion for
woodturning. My career with wood started
at a young age and is always inspired by life’s
simplicity, patterns and textures. While
woodturning has been a longtime love, Paul
Russell Designs is a more recent endeavor as
my work has taken a more serious and artistic turn. I still appreciate my legacy heavy
rustic bowls. However, more recent works
focus on the line of the natural edge bowl,
thin wavy platters, or extreme twig pots
made from limb elbows and bends, or extreme natural trunk shapes. This latter work I
refer to as my Barely There Series – and you
can see why. It all started with a piece of Lilac branch rescued from a firewood pile, becoming the first in the series. The series reveals beauty in the otherwise ugly and unusable, exploiting ideas of negative space,
while utilizing defects and imperfections to
accentuate. Inside is outside!”
It was perhaps Paul’s wonderous way he looks at
wood that caught my attention when I first saw
him demonstrate during the World of Woodturners
Online Symposium in January 2023 that I knew I
wanted to see more and had hoped others in the
GVWG would be curious too. And hearing that he
was someone who learned directly from Dale Nish I
am even more keen to learn more about what Paul
knows.
Breaking into the relatively new method of
offering Interactive Remote
Demos
(IRD’s)
Paul brought his wealth
of turning experience to
our group during our
January 2024 monthly
hybrid meeting where
we had members and
guests both in the Sapperton Hall as well as online
connected via Zoom. A huge thank you to all the
people and crew that made this happen. There is
so much to do to pull it off, but once again a quality
demonstration happened for the GVWG given their
dedication and efforts.
Paul, in our January 2024 meeting and while answering questions during the following Tech Talk
perhaps opened the hearts, minds, and sparked
curiosity for some of the members of the guild.
What are some of the key talking points and take
aways? Let’s review.
Paul shared some of how his Barley There Series
came to be, all because of a lilac burl and his decision to make a twig pot.
He began reviewing how making cuts while at the
tree, changing your cuts with your chainsaw gives
(Continued on page 11)

Dale Nish

other options.
Paul showed some incredible pieces of wood with
possibilities and then he took us through his stepby-step process of considerations and things to
look for to ensure that the piece has good contact
and can be turned safely. His drawing of how the
forces affect the compression of the wood, the
need to have parallel contact points and the importance of using a cup centre and for the Steb
centre having equal application of teeth marks before putting tool to wood were all very instructional key take aways.
The February President’s challenge is “Turning Air”
and throughout Paul’s demonstration we could see
the wood rotating and how we look and can see
the shadows of the wood that is there, and not
there. Visually we identify seeing the “cone” shape
of the spigot or the rounding corner of the base.
Grain orientation comes into play too. There are
times that a pull cut is more appropriate than a
push cut. Once the bulk of the wood was shaped
from the midline, Paul took refining cuts to find a
shape that in his experience works for making his
twig pots. All before making the final parting cut
which was done using his band saw.
One of the things I absolutely love about bringing
in outside demonstrators is their perspective of the
way they choose to do something. It plants a seed
and opens ideas. It helps me question and explore
other possibilities, and it makes me ponder and
challenge those things I have heard on my journey
so far. Early in the demonstration, Paul put on a
glove. This is something I had heard repeatedly
that one never is to do while turning at the lathe.
Paul has his reasons for it, and the precautions he

I was surprised by Paul’s way to remove the nub,

I so appreciated the opportunity to watch the
demonstration again as
I managed to make connections of how a whole
bunch of items in my
possession are connected. Paul shed some
light on seeds previously
planted that is so close to bursting with possibilities. Taking the time to write this newsletter article
was a way to capture and share. Did you have
different nuggets that stood out for you and ignited your own imagination?
While I stepped away
from the official role of
Education Coordinator,
this task still needs to
be
fulfilled
each
meeting. Perhaps you
have an idea of something you want to learn,
or you have seen a demonstrator, project piece, or inspiration from a
completely different source you would like to explore more. This just might be a seed that could
flourish into something others might be interested
in exploring too. Approach the President or any
other board member of the GWVG to see what is
possible with your idea. Perhaps you too will make
a connection you did not realize had the potential
for something very interesting indeed.
And finally, as the maker, you get to decide what is
ugly wood. Hopefully you got some ideas of considerations and tips to safely explore your own
chunk of “Ugly” wood. Looking ahead, GVWG’s Art
Liestman will be at the March meeting doing his
perspective on Twig Pots and the possibility of using this to develop explore form, processes, and
play. Stay tuned for even more possibilities.

As many of you are aware, the floor of the KMS
classroom that the Guild uses for Intro to Turning
and visiting demonstrator classes had become increasingly slippery over the last 18 months reaching the point where it was unsafe and preventing
the Guild from offering Intro to Woodturning classes last fall.
The issue behind the slipperiness links back to a
soap stone turning class a few years ago and had
become progressively worse over subsequent classes. With the blessing of the KMS team, the Guild
undertook the refinishing of the floor.
To ensure we had a workable solution a candidate
Varathane floor finish was first applied to test
patches, both with and without an anti-slip additive called Shark Grip. With help from Linda, Brian L
and Brian’s trusty floor sander, the test patches
were completed last December.
The test patch tria found that:
1. Both Varathane only and Varathane plus Shark
Grip were a significant improvement over the
old floor surface
2. While the patches with Shark Grip were grippier that Varathane only, they also became noticeably dirtier after only minor foot traffic from
removing the lathes in preparation for sanding
the whole floor.
It was decided to go with the Varathane only solution to avoid dirt accumulation and simplify the
application process. We finally managed to get
schedules for a working party to align on Saturday
20th January to sand the floor and apply the floor
finish. Unfortunately, the application had to be
broken into two parts because the workbenches
were too big to move out of the classroom. We
therefore had to play workbench Tetris and finished the first 2/3rds of the floor on Saturday afternoon, before returning the next morning to move
the work benches and complete the remaining section of floor. Huge thanks to Ed P, Brian L and Steve
D for making themselves available both days to
complete the work, and an extra special shout out
to Brian’s wife Wanda for helping Brian apply a second coat to the main floor area late Saturday afternoon.
For the record, and for the technically minded, the
floor was sanded using a drum sander from Home
Depot fitted with a 60 grit belt. The finish used was
Varathane Diamond Premium Polyurethane Wood
Finish for Floors, Water-Based in Satin Clear. Two

The beauty and wonder of the art we produce belies the underlying risk it potentially poses to our
health and safety. While we are mindful of the
need to use and handle equipment safely, we often
fall short when it comes to safeguarding our hearing, eyesight and breathing. If that’s the case for
you here’s some basic personal protection advice
from experienced woodworkers. Embrace what
works best for your work environment and fits
your budget without compromising your health. If
you’d like additional information the American Association of Woodturners carries an excellent video
Personal Protection for Woodturners narrated by
Lauren Zenreich. Posted newsletters with the
Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild and chatlines with the World of Woodturners (WOW) are
also chock-full of information.
Lungs
Threats: Wood dust and other particulates we inhale can compromise our lungs and the effects can
be accumulative, leading to allergic reactions, lung
disease and even cancer. We often think about
visible dust being the primary culprit, but it can be
microscopic particles that pose the gravest threat.
Certain wood dust (exotic and local) can be hazardous and accumulations of dust and shavings can
present a risk of fires or explosions. Dust as we all
know can adhere to our clothing and hair so it is
advisable to keep soiled clothing in the shop and
shower after a dust-laden day. Hazardous chemicals from finishes, solvents, glues and epoxies can
be harmful along with filings from grinding and
smoke from wood burning (pyrography). For brevity purposes dust will be used generically in this
article to represent all harmful airborne materials.
Action suggested: The surest way of keeping our
lungs free of dust entails the wearing of appropriate personal protection equipment and requires
the removal and collection of dust at its source.
For the most part we will need to embrace aspects
of both approaches as dust in woodworking is pervasive. When choosing protection equipment and
products remember that you get what you pay for.
The cheaper options will likely be the least effective and in the case of dust collectors be the noisiest. Be sure to make your purchases from reputable suppliers and buy products that are recognized
by the Canadian Standards Association (CSA) or the
National Institute for Occupational Safety and
Health (NIOSH).
Centralized dust collection (CDC): The central shop
dust collection system consists of a network of hoses that capture dust at its source and route it to a
central vacuum where its contents are stored in
(Continued on page 16)

filter bags or canisters
which are usually located in a designated area
to muffle noise and
contain escaped dust.
Hoses typically run to
stationary
dustgenerating work stations
(lathes,
etc.).
Please note that supplemental
protection
equipment such as a
mask may still be required to capture errant dust. The Cadillac of all
cleaning systems, they are often found in industrial
and teaching venues.
Power tool and hand tool dust collection: Most
new
wood
working
equipment (hand sanders, belt sanders, table
saws, planers, bandsaws, etc.) can be connected to portable shop
vacuums or CDC systems. If you have older
power tools, especially
band saws, you may
want to capture dust
with a magnetized dust
chute or a dust port on
the lower flywheel cover. Dust hoods with a
self-attached
magnets
are commonly used by
turners at the lathe but
also lend themselves to
a variety of shop uses.
All of these items are
available through suppliers like Lee Valley
Tools, KMS Tools and
Grainger Tools. Once
again you may need to
mask up to capture escaped dust. You may
also want to consider doing heavy-duty belt sanding outdoors where possible.
Workbench dust collection: Portable or built in
dust collectors work well for bench top setups, especially for the use of rotary power tools or wood
burners, when placed directly behind or below the
work space to draw dust away from you. You do
not want to draw dust through you on its way to
the collector. A number of commercial portable
dust collectors are available through carving equipment suppliers like Razertip Industries (now Maple
and Brass) and Lee Valley Tools. In this particular
area rotary power carvers have made an assortment of home-made dust collectors which usually
entail the use of furnace filters. They do the job for
light work, but require regular cleaning. Hanging
commercial air cleaners are found in many shops.
They move a huge volume of air and can be left
running to purify the air long after the lights are
turned off. Newer models are remote controlled
with timer and speed settings. Think about placing
these close to your workstation to draw dust away
from you.

Portable Floor Cleaners: These include shop vacuums which we all have and a variety of high efficiency (HEPA) extractors. The latter clean up to
99.5% of particulates and run quieter than shop
vacuums. They also come at a heftier price tag.
Both of these cleaners can be attached to equipment or just used for general shop cleaning.
Wearable gear: Face mask protection is essential
for most wood working.
Disposable dust mask: The N95 disposable mask
(rated for 95% filtration efficiency) is commonplace
today, but for some of
us tends to restrict
breathing and is prone
to fogging eyeglasses
under certain conditions. Both of those
issues are addressed
with the wearing of an
N95 mask with an air
flow valve. Disposable
masks should be snug
and be capable of being shaped around the
nose for a tight fit. Consider storing your open
mask in a Ziploc bag when not in use to keep dust
from settling on it. While not a perfect form of protection the N95 is better than wearing nothing- unless you are sporting a beard and then it is rendered
useless.
Reusable respirator: The half mask respirator is
worn over the mouth and nose. It comes with adjustable straps for a
snug fit and exchangeable filtration cartridges.
Cartridges can perform
designated
functions
(P100 rating is recommended). Keep replacements on hand.
Full face masks are also
available. Be sure to
buy the size that fits
properly. 3M products
come highly recommended for disposable and reusable masks.
Self-contained breathing system: These systems
when fully decked out offer top notch protection
for your lungs, ears and eyes- especially in high
dust production environments. The units fit
over your head and consist of a hooded face
shield and mask that
feeds filtered air over
the face. Air is moved
by a battery-operated
fan. Filter cartridges
capture up to 98% of
dust particles. Air filters and visor overlays
are replaceable. Lee
Valley Tools carries a Trend Airshield Pro model
that is worth checking out, but like all purchases it
is good to shop around (also try Amazon and eBay).
If the model does not provide ear protection look
for an ear muff fitted with a strap-type head band
to wear under the unit.
Eyes
Threats: Unfortunately, eye injuries are all too frequent in the work environment.
Action suggested: For most of us the best way to
protect our eyes is to get into the habit of wearing
safety goggles or safety glasses with side shields. If
you wear regular eyeglasses consider getting safety
googles with prescription lens or safety goggles
that fit over your glasses (although these may be
prone to fogging). If
fogging is an issue or
you are potentially in
the path of blunt force
hits (turners in particular) consider using a full
-face shield rated for
impact
protection.
Please note that splash
shields only protect you
from
errant
liquids.
Purchase a face shield

that fits securely and is
adjustable. Buy replacement visors so you
have them when needed. If you are a rotary
tool power carver or a
pyrographer who works
from a bench you can
protect your face by
using a LED magnifying

undertaking detail work.
Ears
Threats: As we age our hearing- like our eyesight-
tends to deteriorate. Damaged ears do not repair
themselves.
Action suggested: The best way to protect our
ears is to wear quality well fitted (over the head)
ear muffs. Some respirator helmet systems accommodate ear muffs. Noise canceling ear buds are
gaining popularity in the work place and may be
worth considering, especially if they are custom fit
by a specialist. In a pinch disposable ear plugs may
prove useful, but should not be considered an ideal
means of protection.
Hands and Feet
Threats: Our hands and feet are on the front line
in the work environment and open to injury.
Action suggested: The best way to protect our
hands is to wear gloves- plain and simple. Buy
gloves appropriate to the task and have them within reach at all times. You can buy gloves that are
cut resistant, heat resistant and appropriate for
using chainsaws. For most general workshop activity light well fitted leather gloves will go a long way
in protecting your hands. Disposable latex gloves
are an asset when handing most glues and finishes.
If you are allergic to latex gloves or looking for
more durable handwear (epoxy use etc.) consider
buying nitrile gloves. Glove use draws a mixed response from woodturners. Some turners shun
gloves, fearful of having
fingers/hands caught by
turning
equipment.
Others will wear open
finger gloves to deflect
flying wood chips and
maintain a feel for the
wood. Open finger gloves can be purchased or
fashioned out of regular gloves by cutting off the
finger portions at the first knuckle from the palm.
Avoid any kind of rubber, cloth or flimsy glove in
turning.
The best way to protect our feet is to wear
appropriate footwear
especially
when
it
comes to using a chainsaw or any other tool
capable of removing
body parts. Along that
line protective legwear
is also highly recommended.

unexpected.
And I then responded, “a
really good teacher to
patiently show you the

While Gary Burns had me

October
2023.
Dan
learned from Jay Mapson. And Jay’s foray

while

Yes, this is the same

There are lots of fabulous resources and tools for

Which pen kit will you use? The pen kit selected
will influence a whole bunch of decisions including
the size and length of your blank, your bushings,
your mandrel (or no mandrel) options and even
your wood, resin, blank selection. Often these kits
come with different nib and clip colours…but the
colour matters less at this moment of the process.
For example, if you buy a bunch of “slimline” kits,
you can cut the blanks, and do the process of the
preparing the blank, trimming them, and even turn
and finish all before you need to select which
“colour” to use for your assembled pen. This is
where it can be super helpful to pick a style you
like so you can make many pens all with the same
process and in the final steps select the accessories

The Maxwood Slimline Pen
turning kit is your most economical option and a good
place to start for practicing
the process. The Slimline
requires, a pen blank, a
bushing set (MW-5029), a 7
mm drill bit, a barrel trimmer (MW-BTK), a mandrel, and the tubes that
come with the kit (MW-4994). This pen has two
tubes, one for the top where the clip will be, and
one for the bottom where the nib is located. The
stock codes given are from KMS and William Wood
-Write has different SKU for the similar items.
Alternatively, the Elegant Pen turning kit
requires a bushing set
(MW-4980), a 10 mm
drill bit, a barrel trimmer (MW-BTK)…same
barrel trimmer, but a
different size within
the kit, and a mandrel,
or one can get away
without a mandrel if
they have a way to
hold it between centres as this is a single barrel
pen, and the tube that comes with the kit (MW5181).
Confused and overwhelmed yet? I was. There are
lots of different options and pen kit styles, but the
process and gear required essentially remains the
same. The drill bit size and the appropriate bushing size and configuration are the things that are
most important and will vary, depending on the kit
you decide to use.
Both KMS and William-Wood Write have a dizzying
number of options…and there are so many more
options if you go down south to Rockler, Penstate
or even Craft Supplies. Each website also has a
wealth of information of what you will require for
each specific kit as well as detailed instructions. Be
sure to check them out. And there are endless
YouTube videos too.
If you selected a kit with
two sides, you would
want to use a mandrel. If
you have a single tube,
you could choose to secure your blank between
centres
using
a
60degree hardened steel
metal lathe drive centre.
I personally use the mandrel…but can appreciate
that there are pros and
cons
to
each
option….and I have yet to
acquire a harden steel
drive centre. Bushing
placement can matter,
especially if the kit has
multiple bushings sizes
within the same pen kit. For the Slimline kit, they
are all 7 mm. One may want to add more bushings
at the headstock and tailstock ends to give yourself
more clearance. Other pen kits may require different bushings…and the order of the bushings may
matter. This is where beginner pen turners may
want to pick a kit and stick with it for a while before branching out. Thoroughly reading the instructions available can help too.
Sanding and finishing have its own list of items you
may want in your toolkit too. There is a wide variety of abrasives with wide range of grits (320 -
12,000), different grits for wet
sanding, CA glue for finish, oil
to bring out the grain, HUT
Ultra Gloss or car polish are all
items to consider having at
hand. Some turners minimize
this process while others take
it to a whole different level.

To summarize, here are things you may want for
making a pen:
•
Pen kit (Which one? Dealer’s choice)
•
Drill bit, appropriate size for the pen kit barrel
•
Jacobs chuck & pin jaws to hold the material
and complete the drilling process, others prefer
completing this process using a drill press and

•
Bushings, appropriate for the pen kit
•
Glue (30 minute epoxy or CA glue, give consideration to what works best given your blank)
•
Barrel trimmer (a set will contain multiple sizes,

Mandrel, or a way to hold between centres,

•
Thin CA glue – if this is the finish you want
•

•
Sandpaper, very fine grit to get to the polish
and luster you desire
•
Sheet of plastic to protect your ways during the
glue process
•
Pen press (option as it is possible to do directly
using your lathe)

Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
I have a background in the Arts, construction and
architectural engineering. My brother-in-law Bruce,
who lives in upstate New York, introduced me to
woodturning. He thought I would enjoy it because
of my interest in wood, construction and architecture. He also thought it would easy for me to learn
because I enjoyed using power tools. He has a
great workshop to work in and most of my visits
have included learning something new.
Tell us about your workshop/studio.
I have a somewhat small workshop and it is unheated. It is not usable all year around. Once I decided to buy a lathe, I started converting my gardening/tool and bike storage area (under the front
porch of an older Victorian style house.)
The space is about 8 x 25 and still has most of my
tools and some storage. It originally had bikes and
gardening tools; these have been moved to other
outdoor sheds.
I have been working on a second workshop on my
property on the Sunshine Coast. It is a larger space
but is also unheated and off the power grid so has
other challenges. My property is one of my primary sources for wood.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
My favourite tool is most likely my ½-bowl gouge.

Free wood (LOL). I like working with wood and try
hard to find different kinds of wood to turn.

part of deciding what I am going to turn.
Hard to actually say what my favourite wood is. I
most often turn bowls and use big leaf maple because I have and can get it easily, and it is free. I do
like turning dogwood, arbutus, and black locust.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

Page 45
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
